newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's AIB to buy US bank for $1.36 bln.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's AIB to buy US bank for $1.36 bln.

text.p: Allied Irish Banks Plc said on Tuesday that its U.S. unit First Maryland Bancorp (FMB) had agreed to buy Dauphin Deposit Corp for $1.36 billion, the biggest acquistion ever made by an Irish company.
AIB said Dauphin, a bank holding company with headquarters in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, was a "low risk acquisition" that fit neatly into its U.S. expansion plans.

"It's a terrific deal from our perspective. It's a quality institution which ties in terrifically well with FMB and will result in FMB becoming the 45th largest bank in the whole of the U.S.," AIB chief executive Tom Mulcahy told a news conference.

Under the terms of the agreement, Dauphin shareholders may elect to exchange each share they hold for $43 in cash or an equivalent value of AIB's American Depositary Receipts, each of which represent six ordinary shares of AIB.
The board of Dauphin, the fourth largest Pennsylvania commercial bank with about $6.0 billion in assets, has agreed to recommend the offer to shareholders.

"Of all the options we considered, the AIB combination presented the best alternative for continued growth for shareholders, access to the technology which will enable us to growt our business and the most favourable long-term career opportunities for our constituencies," Dauphin chairman and chief executive Christopher Jennings said.
AIB expects to close the acquisition during the third quarter of 1997 and will fund it from existing resources.

In conjunction with the acquisition, the Irish bank will also seek approval from its shareholders to purchase up to 50 million of its ordinary shares in the open market in order to reduce its surplus capital to normal after the transaction.

Dauphin provides a full line of retail, commercial, trust and other financial services and operates 98 branches in south central Pennsylvania. It reported an eight percent increase in net income to $71 million in 1996.

AIB said it expected to achieve cost savings of up to $48 million per annum within two years of completion as a result of a 28 percent reduction in costs, mainly from duplicative corporate overheads and administrative functions.
The Irish bank will take a restructuring charge of $60 million in 1997 because of conversion and severance costs.

As a result, the acquisition should be earnings neutral for AIB in 1997, moderately accretive in 1998 and significantly accretive in 1999 and beyond. AIB's share price closed 10 pence lower in Dublin on Tuesday at 407 Irish pence per share.
